For an AI enabled nanosatellite for QKD, design engineers must trade the often-conflicting requirements of space, cybersecurity, AI and quantum to progress the design from the complex to the merely complicated.

In the initial phases agile principles are employed, allowing for experimentation in design. With increasing knowledge of the problem space, there is a reduction in the uncertainty in design elements, leading to a transition from an agile based lifecycle to the waterfall-based methods more suitable for Flight Model implementation.

Underpinning the project is a Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach. Enterprise Architect was selected as the MBSE tool of choice during blue sky design stages, allowing a smooth transition from capability level considerations to systems and subsystems design.

The Zachman framework offers a consistent, but potentially over flexible, approach to model development. MBSE offers a clear methodology for integrating the model with external simulation tools to provide on ground verification of platform behaviours and porting design effort to support new mission concepts.

The application of flexibility in lifecycle management, sound security principles and a model-based approach to technical development has proven to be a highly effective approach in increasing our understanding of complex systems allowing for complicated, but mature, designs to be defined.
The initial service implementation is based on a technology demonstration through the 'Responsive Operations for Key Services' (ROKS) satellite to be launched in 2022.
To address this focus was placed on a structured approached based on Model Based Systems Engineering. This allows the translation of the design from 'blue sky' concept to implemented subsystems.
For the ROKS project the Enterprise Architect MBSE tool was selected due to it extension packages for Enterprise Architecture alongside SysML functions.

In order to support the Model Based approach the Zachman Framework for Enterprise Architecture was selected to structure development. This allowed for the project to begin by answering high level questions around the business case for QKD as a nascent market, before flowing business considerations into the systems design itself through various levels of instantiation.
Through the tool traceability is managed, ensuring requirement flow down from capability level to subsystem level.

The use of Enterprise Architect supports design decomposition. The models' behavioural views enforce an approach which considers the structural and behavioural architectural elements in parallel. This ensures equal focus is placed on the functional (e.g. software) as well as physical (e.g. hardware) design.
Through the use of MBSE approaches the complexity associated with the development of a multifaceted satellite-based service was managed and the effort associated with doing so was reduced.

This allows the use of untrusted 3rd party avionics (e.g. an 'Off The Shelf' satellite bus) but also means that the payload itself can be deployed on platforms such as High Altitude Pseudo Satellites (HAPS) and also as a secondary payload on a separate satellite platform.

Here neural networks are deployed on standard space-based hardware which can detect and geolocate cloud using a low performance imager. Due to the decision to develop the payload in isolation from the platform this functionality must be payload hosted. This creates a situation where a payload must task the platform avionics (i.e. the main On Board Computer - OBC).

Based on significant desk-based research and work with security orientated partners an approach which combined a number of separate standards into a bespoke framework was defined. Examples of standards which were incorporated includes ISO:27001 [2] for general company system and facility security, CCSDS [3] for space specific considerations, ETSI developments towards a standard suite for QKD [4] systems and even British Standards around Automotive and Control Systems for device level considerations [5].
This consolidation of requirements ensures that security concepts are flown into the design at all levels and a comprehensive approach is taken.
This platform is based on the purchase of a Commercial Off The Shelf (COTS) nanosatellite platform, with a payload consisting of a number of key subsystems.
At the time of authorship, the Flight Model platform is in development, with launch set for late 2022.

While the use of Model Based Systems Engineering has been a significant success, the implementation of the Zachman Framework was noted to create a number of arbitrary tasks which did not influence the design process. Here more flexibility in deployment, or potentially consideration of more widely used frameworks (such as TOGAF [7]) may have improved design efficiency.
This approach could be further refined towards a baseline for future space based cyber security services.

By focusing on the functional architecture early in the project the operation of autonomous elements could be understood, and its impact on other subsystems defined. This has allowed the definition and implementation of a novel approach to cloud detection which allows for targeted downlink of optical communications data based on local weather conditions.
The above has facilitated the development of a mission concept and requisite subsystems for QKD demonstration from nanosatellite.
